title: 22. Interview: What is System Design?
summary: Interview Q&A for What is System Design? — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 What is System Design? interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is the difference between system design and system architecture?
**Answer:** System architecture describes the static structure of a system — which components exist, what their responsibilities are, and how they are connected (for example: "API gateway → service mesh → microservices → managed Postgres with read replicas"). System design is the broader, dynamic activity that produces that architecture: gathering requirements, estimating capacity, choosing components, evaluating trade-offs, and iterating under failure and load. Architecture is the noun; design is the verb. A useful analogy: architecture is the blueprint of a building, while design also includes deciding whether the building needs elevators at all, how many people it must hold, and what happens during a fire. In interviews, "design X" usually means walk me through both — the components and the reasoning that picked them — not just sketch a box diagram and stop.

**Visual:**
```
+-----------------+        +-------------------+
| System Design   |  -->   | System            |
| (the process)   |        | Architecture      |
| - requirements  |        | (the artifact)    |
| - estimates     |        | - components      |
| - trade-offs    |        | - connections     |
+-----------------+        +-------------------+
```

### Q2. Why do interviewers say there is "no right answer" in system design?
**Answer:** Because every concrete design is a bundle of trade-offs, and which trade-off is acceptable depends on requirements the interviewer has not fully stated. Saying "use Kafka" is neither right nor wrong until you know the write throughput, the latency budget, the operational capacity of the team, and the consistency needs. Interviewers reward candidates who expose and justify trade-offs more than those who pick a "fancy" stack. The hidden evaluation criteria are usually: can you decompose ambiguity, can you estimate capacity, can you reason about failure modes, and can you accept a constraint and re-design rather than freeze? The "no right answer" framing also reflects that real production systems ship many different architectures for the same problem — Twitter, Facebook, and Instagram all run global social graphs with materially different storage and fan-out choices.

**Visual:**
```
       Decision points (each is a trade-off)
       +------> SQL vs NoSQL
       |
Req ---+------> Sync vs Async
       |
       +------> Cache-aside vs Write-through
       |
       +------> Single region vs Multi-region
```

### Q3. What is the "scale ladder" and why is it useful?
**Answer:** The scale ladder is a mental model that maps user counts to typical architectures: 1 user (laptop + SQLite), 1K users (single server + Postgres), 1M users (load balancer + cache + read replicas), 1B users (multi-region active-active + sharded storage + tiered caches). It is useful because it tells you how far ahead to design. A startup at 1K users should not build a 100-service mesh; the operational cost will sink them. Conversely, a system at 100M users cannot survive on a single primary database. The ladder prevents two classic mistakes: over-engineering for a scale you will never reach, and under-engineering for a scale you will reach next quarter. A good rule of thumb is to design for roughly 10x current load — enough headroom to survive a viral spike and enough runway to plan the next migration.

**Visual:**
```
1 user      : [ laptop + sqlite ]
1K users    : [ 1 server + 1 DB ]
1M users    : [ LB + cache + replicas ]
1B users    : [ multi-region active-active, sharded ]
                  ^
                  | design ~1 rung ahead
```

### Q4. What is back-of-the-envelope estimation and what numbers should you always compute?
**Answer:** Back-of-the-envelope estimation is rough arithmetic — accurate to one significant digit — used to size a system before drawing components. The four numbers every designer should compute are: (1) QPS, split into read and write, with peak ≈ 3× average; (2) storage per day and per year, including replication and retention; (3) bandwidth in Mbps at peak; (4) cache hit rate required to meet the latency budget. These four numbers drive every downstream decision: number of DB shards, number of cache nodes, CDN egress cost, and whether a single Kafka partition can keep up. Without them, "do we shard?" is a debate; with them, it is division. The other reason to do estimates aloud in an interview is that they expose hidden requirements — for example, realizing that the write QPS is higher than a single Postgres primary can handle reframes the entire design.

**Visual:**
```
Inputs                Computation              Output
----------            -------------            ------
DAU = 50M             50M * 30 / 86400         QPS_avg = 17K
peak = 3x             17K * 3                   QPS_peak = 51K
write ratio = 1/11    51K / 11                  Write QPS = 4.6K
payload = 1KB         4.6K * 86400 * 1KB        Storage/day = 380 GB
```

### Q5. How does Twitter's architecture evolution illustrate system design principles?
**Answer:** Twitter started as a Rails monolith on MySQL — the simplest design that could ship. That choice was correct for ~10K users. As traffic grew, the timeline fan-out query (`SELECT * FROM tweets WHERE author IN (...) ORDER BY time`) became the bottleneck, because each user followed hundreds of people. Twitter first shard MySQL by user id, then introduced a hybrid push/pull fan-out: tweets from celebrities are pulled, tweets from normal users are pushed into per-user timeline lists. They later rewrote the timeline service on the JVM for GC predictability and built Gizzard for sharded MySQL and Manhattan for a distributed key-value store. Each step was a trade-off: simplicity was traded for capacity, latency, or operational cost. The lesson is that system design is iterative — the "right" architecture at month 6 is wrong at month 36, and the cost of migrating between them is itself a design input.

**Visual:**
```
2006:  [ Rails monolith ] --> [ MySQL (primary) ]
2010:  [ Rails ] --> [ Sharded MySQL ] --> [ Memcached ]
2015:  [ JVM timeline svc ] --> [ Manhattan KV ] --> [ Gizzard shards ]
```

### Q6. What is "resume-driven design" and how do you avoid it?
**Answer:** Resume-driven design is choosing technologies because they look impressive on a CV rather than because they fit the problem — for example, picking Kafka, Kubernetes, and Cassandra for an internal CRM used by 50 people. It is avoided by starting from requirements and capacity estimates, then picking the simplest technology that meets the numbers with ~10x headroom. The cost of a wrong simple choice is a migration; the cost of a wrong complex choice is operational toil, on-call burnout, and bugs in technologies the team does not fully understand. A useful test: for every component, write the one sentence that justifies its existence relative to a simpler alternative. If the sentence is "it scales better" but your QPS is 50, delete the component. The best designers are ruthless about deleting boxes, not adding them.

**Visual:**
```
Resume-driven            Requirement-driven
--------------------     --------------------
Kafka + K8s + Cass       Postgres + cron + nginx
For a 50-user CRM        For a 50-user CRM
(operational cost: high) (operational cost: low)
```

### Q7. How does system design differ from algorithm design?
**Answer:** Algorithm design focuses on a single computation: given an input, find the most efficient sequence of steps to produce an output, measured in time and space complexity. System design focuses on a distributed collection of components that must cooperate under concurrency, failure, and growth, measured in latency, throughput, availability, and cost. An algorithm is correct or incorrect; a system is "good enough" or "not good enough" given trade-offs. Algorithm problems usually have a single optimal answer (e.g., the O(n log n) sort); system problems rarely do. In interviews, algorithm rounds test coding speed and correctness; system design rounds test communication, decomposition, and judgment under ambiguity. Both matter: a system with a poor algorithm at its core will not scale, and a great algorithm wrapped in a poor system will not stay up.

**Visual:**
```
Algorithm design           System design
---------------------      -----------------------
input -> output            many components, many users
measures: O(time, space)   measures: latency, throughput, avail
one optimal answer         many acceptable trade-offs
machine is honest          network lies, disks fail
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your startup's blog went viral on Hacker News and traffic jumped from 100 req/s to 8,000 req/s. The site is now returning 502s. Walk me through how you think about this as a system design problem.
**Answer:** First, I would not redesign the whole system — I would stabilize, then diagnose. Stabilization: put a CDN (Cloudflare or CloudFront) in front with aggressive caching for static assets and a short TTL for HTML; this typically cuts origin traffic by 80–90%. If the origin still dies, I would vertically scale the single web server (bigger box) because that is the fastest move; horizontal scaling takes longer because of state and deployment. Diagnosis in parallel: which component is the bottleneck — CPU on the web tier, connection pool exhaustion on the DB, or bandwidth? I would check the four golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation). If the DB is saturated, I would add a read replica and route reads to it. After stabilization, I would treat this as a design signal: the system needs a load balancer, horizontal web tier, read replica, and a cache — but I would not build them all in the middle of the outage. The lesson is that design and operations are linked: every incident is a design feedback loop.

**Visual:**
```
Stabilize:        CDN (cache HTML/static) -> [ web box (2x CPU) ] -> [ DB read replica ]
Diagnose:         check CPU, conn pool, bandwidth
Design follow-up: LB + N web nodes + Redis + read replicas
```

### Q2. You are designing a parking-lot management SaaS for a city with 200 lots. What does "system design" mean for this problem, and what is the simplest acceptable architecture?
**Answer:** System design here means: identify the functional requirements (track occupancy, charge drivers, alert operators), the non-functional requirements (latency for gate-open < 500 ms, availability during network partitions to a lot, retention of payment records for 7 years for audit), then size the load. With 200 lots × maybe 100 spaces × 5 events/space/day = 100K events/day, peak QPS is trivially small — well under 100. The simplest acceptable architecture is one API server (or even a serverless function), one managed Postgres, and a small object store for camera snapshots. I would explicitly NOT introduce Kafka, Kubernetes, or Cassandra — the operational cost dwarfs the benefit. I would design for failure of the lot-to-cloud link by putting a small edge device at each lot that buffers events locally and syncs when the network returns. The hard part of this system is the physical world (gates, cameras, offline operation), not the cloud architecture.

**Visual:**
```
+--------+     +-----------+     +------------------+
| Lot    | --> | Edge box  | --> | API (serverless) |
| gate   |     | (buffer)  |     +--------+---------+
+--------+     +-----------+              |
                                          v
                                  +----------------+
                                  | Managed PG     |
                                  | + S3 snapshots |
                                  +----------------+
```

### Q3. A PM asks you to "design Netflix." Where do you start, and how do you keep the scope manageable?
**Answer:** I start by refusing to design all of Netflix — I scope down to one slice, typically playback, because that is the part with the hardest NFRs. I clarify the functional scope: browse catalog, pick a title, start playback, resume across devices. I clarify the non-functional scope: 99.99% availability, <100 ms playback startup latency, support for 200M+ concurrent streams globally, and bitrate adaptation. Then I do back-of-the-envelope estimates: at 200M concurrent streams × 3 Mbps, that is 600 Tbps of egress — which immediately forces a CDN-first design, because no single origin could serve that. I would propose: clients hit a route service that picks the nearest CDN edge (Open Connect appliance or third-party CDN), the origin only handles manifest generation and personalization, and playback state is stored in a low-latency KV store (Cassandra-style) for resume-across-devices. I would explicitly defer recommendations, billing, and encoding pipelines to separate design sessions. Scoping is itself a system-design skill.

**Visual:**
```
Client -> Route Service -> [Nearest CDN edge (Open Connect)]
                              |
                              v (manifest / personalization only)
                          Origin: API + Cassandra (playback state)
```

### Q4. You inherited a 5-year-old monolith that the team wants to "redesign into microservices." How do you approach this as a system design problem?
**Answer:** I would push back on the framing. Microservices are a deployment and team-scaling optimization, not a goal in themselves. I would first measure: what is actually painful — deploy time, team coordination, scaling of one specific component, or a reliability problem? If the pain is "deploys are slow," a monolith with better CI may be cheaper than a rewrite. If the pain is "the recommendation component needs to scale 50x more than the rest," then splitting that one service out is justified. I would apply the strangler-fig pattern: pick one well-bounded slice (e.g., payments), extract it behind an API, route traffic via a gateway, and operate both in parallel for a migration window. I would explicitly avoid a big-bang rewrite — those almost always fail. The system-design lens here is: treat the existing monolith as a constraint, identify the smallest valuable boundary, and migrate incrementally with reversible steps. Each extraction is itself a small system-design exercise with its own requirements, trade-offs, and SLAs.

**Visual:**
```
            +-----------------+
traffic --->| API Gateway     |--- monolith (still serves most paths)
            +-----------------+--- extracted payments svc (new)
                       ^              |
                       |              v
                  strangler fig   new DB (synced via dual-write or CDC)
```

### Q5. You are designing a feature-flag service that 500 internal services will call. Latency must be under 5 ms p99 and availability 99.99%. Walk me through the design trade-offs.
**Answer:** Five ms p99 rules out a synchronous network hop to a central database on every request — a single cache miss would blow the budget. I would design for in-process evaluation: each service gets a flag-config SDK that fetches the entire flag set (a few hundred KB) into local memory and refreshes it every few seconds via a fan-out mechanism (long-poll, SSE, or a message bus). The central service is only responsible for serving config snapshots and accepting updates from operators — its QPS is ~500 (one per service), not the user-facing QPS. Availability is achieved because once a service has the config in memory, it can keep evaluating flags even if the central service is down (eventual consistency on updates, which is fine for flags). Trade-offs accepted: a flag change can take up to N seconds to propagate, and a bad config pushed to clients could break callers — so I would add versioning, canary rollouts, and a kill switch. This is the classic "fat client, thin server" pattern used by Netflix's Archaius and LaunchDarkly's SDK.

**Visual:**
```
[ Flag admin UI ] --> [ Flag service ] -- fan-out (SSE/poll) -->
                                                          |
   +------------------------------------------------------+
   |              |              |              |
[ svc A ]     [ svc B ]      [ svc C ]     [ svc D ]
  local eval   local eval    local eval    local eval
  <1 ms        <1 ms         <1 ms         <1 ms
```

### Q6. Your team is designing a real-time leader-board for a mobile game with 10M concurrent players. What are the first three design questions you ask?
**Answer:** (1) What is the time window — global all-time, daily, weekly, per-tournament? This drives whether I need a sliding-window structure or a periodic snapshot. (2) How fresh must the top-N be — every write, every second, every minute? Freshness drives whether I can batch updates. (3) What is the read pattern — does every player read their own rank, or only the top 100? Most reads are "my rank and the players around me," which a sorted set (Redis ZSET) handles natively in O(log N). For 10M players, a single Redis ZSET fits in memory (roughly 200 MB), but write QPS may exceed one node — so I would shard by tournament id and possibly use a write buffer that flushes every second. The trade-off: a 1-second flush means a player may briefly see a stale rank, which is almost always acceptable for a game. If I had to support per-player rank for 1B players, I would switch to an approximate structure (HyperLogLog or Count-Min) or a tiered approach.

**Visual:**
```
Player write -> [ buffer (1s flush) ] -> [ Redis ZSET (sharded by tour) ]
                                                    |
Player read  -------- "my rank" ------------------> ZREVRANGE with-score
                    "top 100" ---------------------> ZREVRANGE 0 99
```

### Q7. You are asked to "design Uber." It is too big to design in one hour — how do you decompose it?
**Answer:** I would name the major subsystems up front — rider app, driver app, dispatch, pricing, maps, payments, fraud, notifications — and then ask the interviewer which slice to design. In a real interview I would typically pick dispatch, because it has the hardest real-time constraints. For dispatch I would clarify the requirements: match a rider to the nearest available driver in <5 s, support 10M+ concurrent trips globally, handle driver movement and cancellations, and remain consistent under network partitions. Then I would sketch: rider request hits a regional dispatch service that queries a geospatial index (Redis GEO or a custom quadtree) for nearby drivers, sends offers to the top-K drivers via WebSocket, and assigns on first accept. State (driver location, trip status) lives in a low-latency in-memory store with persistence; the geospatial index is updated continuously by driver pings. The decomposition itself is the system-design skill: large systems are designed slice by slice, and being explicit about which slice you are designing prevents hand-waving.

**Visual:**
```
Uber (the whole company)
 |
 +-- rider app        \___
 +-- driver app        \___  scope of one design session
 +-- maps             /
 +-- pricing         /
 +-- payments        \
 +-- fraud            \_____ explicitly deferred
 +-- notifications    /
 +-- DISPATCH  <== pick this one
        |
        v
   regional dispatch -> geospatial index -> driver WebSockets
```
